title: Run the first Next.js change window

bridge.applicationConcept: Branch, commit, pull request, preview, merge, and revert
bridge.analogyLimit: A pull request also validates user value, accessibility, and maintainability; it is not only an infrastructure change record.

buildBrief: Fork the program, open the onboarding Next.js lab in StackBlitz, change the operator handoff message through GitHub's web editor, create a focused branch, and submit the change through a pull request.
incidentBrief: A conflicting handoff edit and a harmless bad merged message simulate an unsafe change. Resolve the conflict, show the resulting diff, and use GitHub's Revert action without deleting history.
instructions: Create `lab-00-approved` and `lab-00-conflict` from the same unchanged `main` branch; edit the same handoff line differently on each branch through GitHub's web editor.
Preview a branch by replacing `/tree/main` in the StackBlitz URL with `/tree/BRANCH_NAME`; use its terminal for the baseline and incident commands.
Merge the approved PR first, open the conflict PR second, use GitHub's conflict editor to preserve the approved message, and explain each marker before committing the resolution.
Create and merge one separate harmless bad-message PR, then use its GitHub Revert action and merge the generated revert PR to restore the accepted message.

scenario.symptoms: The incident check reports a conflicting and unsafe handoff message.
scenario.reset: Use the merged pull request's Revert action and merge the generated revert pull request

acceptanceTests: The Next.js page renders the approved handoff message
The pull request shows coherent commits and a resolved conflict
A revert restores the last accepted behavior without rewriting history
evidence: Before, conflict, resolution, and revert screenshots
predictionQuestions: Which repository and branch will change after each action?
What history will remain after revert compared with deleting the commit?
defenseQuestions: Trace the change from browser edit to merged repository state.
Explain fork, clone, branch, commit, pull request, merge, and revert in your own words.
Show one controlled text change without asking Codex to regenerate the page.
hints: Draw the canonical repository, your fork, and the two browser branches as separate boxes before editing.
Compare both sides of the conflict marker and restate the desired final sentence.
Use a new commit that reverses the bad commit; do not erase shared history.

title: Diagnose the Codex and Vercel toolchain

bridge.applicationConcept: Codex context, local CLIs, deployment inspection, and evidence boundaries
bridge.analogyLimit: A CLI may have write privileges and cloud credentials; it is not inherently a read-only management plane.

buildBrief: Complete a tool-access matrix, add project AGENTS.md guidance, deploy the practice app, and use Codex plus Vercel CLI evidence to explain the deployment state.
incidentBrief: The preview build receives a deliberately missing public configuration name. Diagnose the build log, distinguish build-time from runtime state, and make the smallest safe correction.

scenario.symptoms: The preview reports a missing NEXT_PUBLIC training variable and shows which phase read it.

acceptanceTests: Codex reports the intended repository instructions
The tool matrix separates read, write, authentication, sensitive data, and revocation
The deployment diagnosis cites a specific safe log line and focused diff
predictionQuestions: Which tool can observe the deployment and which can mutate it?
At what phase is each environment value read?
defenseQuestions: Explain why Codex must start in the correct repository.
Compare a CLI, API, SDK, plugin, MCP server, and documentation site.
Identify one tool permission you would revoke after the exercise.
hints: Ask each tool what it can read, write, and authenticate to.
Search the first relevant build error rather than the final generic failure line.
Match the variable name and environment before changing application code.

title: Select and defend an accessible UI system

bridge.applicationConcept: Design tokens, accessible primitives, interaction states, and component ownership
bridge.analogyLimit: UI libraries can be mixed technically, but mismatched behavior and visual rules still create a poor and inaccessible product.

buildBrief: First express the AtlasOps status-panel outcome as a compact visual Markdown story. Then compare status cards, tables, dialogs, forms, badges, and feedback states from the curated libraries and implement one coherent panel using shared tokens.
incidentBrief: The supplied panel clips at mobile width and exposes a keyboard-inaccessible details control. Repair both while preserving the selected visual direction.
instructions: Before implementation, use the visual story-writing guide and agency story template to define the panel outcome, acceptance examples, UI states, failure path, and smallest useful Mermaid flow. Render and critique the packet with Codex.

scenario.symptoms: The accessibility and responsive checks report an unnamed control and horizontal overflow.

acceptanceTests: A rendered Markdown story defines the user outcome, Given/When/Then behavior, boundaries, non-goals, evidence, and a labeled flow with a text route
The component comparison records license, ownership, accessibility, bundle, and maintenance tradeoffs
The selected panel uses one token system and works at mobile, tablet, and desktop widths
Keyboard focus and non-color status labels are observable
evidence: Rendered visual story, three component comparisons, and selected ADR
Mobile, tablet, desktop, and keyboard captures
predictionQuestions: Which user outcome does this panel deliver, and which implementation work does not belong in the story headline?
Which component behavior comes from a primitive and which comes from local styling?
What will happen to the table and actions below 375 pixels?
defenseQuestions: Defend the story slice, observable acceptance examples, and selected diagram.
Name the layout, hierarchy, density, rhythm, and feedback decisions.
Explain why the chosen libraries can coexist coherently.
Modify one component state without regenerating the panel.
hints: Inspect semantics and keyboard behavior before visual polish.
Use shared tokens for spacing, radius, color, and focus instead of per-component guesses.
Test the narrowest viewport and zoom before declaring the layout responsive.

title: Recover a responsive vertical slice

bridge.applicationConcept: Responsive layout, component state, wrapping, and overflow
bridge.analogyLimit: A viewport is not a network link; content priority and human comprehension matter more than raw fitting capacity.

buildBrief: Implement the approved ClearPath service section as a responsive Next.js component with semantic structure, reusable props, and explicit loading-independent content.
incidentBrief: A fixed minimum width and non-wrapping action row cause horizontal overflow. Use browser evidence to identify the owning rule and repair it without redesigning the section.

scenario.symptoms: The 320-pixel viewport test reports horizontal overflow and a clipped secondary action.

acceptanceTests: The vertical slice matches the approved content hierarchy
No horizontal overflow occurs from 320 pixels through desktop widths
You identify the exact component and CSS rule responsible
predictionQuestions: Which element do you expect to define the minimum page width?
Will wrapping, shrinking, or clipping best preserve content priority?
defenseQuestions: Trace props into rendered semantic HTML and styles.
Explain why the failing rule affected the whole page.
Change one breakpoint behavior without rewriting the component.
hints: Find the widest element before editing media queries.
Inspect min-width, white-space, flex-wrap, and child shrink behavior.
Prefer a layout rule that works across widths over a single device patch.

title: Restore a failed client form launch

bridge.applicationConcept: Browser/server boundaries, environment configuration, form validation, and provider failure
bridge.analogyLimit: A successful deployment only proves artifacts were released; it does not prove the user workflow or external provider succeeded.

buildBrief: Complete a validated ClearPath contact flow with accessible feedback, a server-only email adapter, synthetic analytics, and local, preview, and production configuration notes.
incidentBrief: Preview validation succeeds in the browser but submission fails because server configuration is missing and the client attempts to read a secret. Restore the correct boundary and user-safe failure state.

scenario.symptoms: Submission returns a safe configuration error while the boundary check detects secret access in client code.

acceptanceTests: Invalid forms explain the exact correction and focus the relevant field
Only the server adapter reads the synthetic email credential
Preview failure returns a useful retry or contact alternative without exposing configuration
predictionQuestions: Which validation must happen in both browser and server?
Which environment names may reach the browser and which values must remain server-only?
defenseQuestions: Trace submission from field input through server adapter and response.
Explain why a public prefix changes the secret boundary.
Demonstrate rollback to the last working deployment.
hints: Separate user input validation from provider configuration validation.
Search the client bundle boundary for the credential name, not its value.
Return a stable user message while logging a safe operational category.

title: Qualify an unreliable AtlasOps provider

bridge.applicationConcept: HTTP authentication, status codes, rate limits, timeouts, payload validation, and provider evaluation
bridge.analogyLimit: An HTTP status alone rarely establishes business cause; provider documentation, headers, payloads, and product context are also required.

buildBrief: Define AtlasOps service-health requirements, compare three providers from official documentation, test synthetic requests, and propose a provider-independent internal contract.
incidentBrief: The provider fixture rotates through 401, 429, timeout, and malformed JSON. Classify each failure, choose safe retry behavior, and preserve a usable product state.

scenario.symptoms: Four synthetic provider modes produce distinct authentication, quota, transport, and contract failures.

acceptanceTests: Three providers are compared with official docs, cost, rights, limits, support, and exit risk
The adapter distinguishes 401, 429, timeout, malformed payload, and empty success
The ADR defines retry, cache, fallback, and stop conditions
predictionQuestions: Which failures are safe to retry automatically?
Which response details must be validated before the UI trusts the payload?
defenseQuestions: Explain authentication, authorization, transport, quota, and schema failures.
Trace one provider response into the normalized contract.
Defend when AtlasOps should stop using the provider.
hints: Classify the layer before changing retry behavior.
Read status, headers, body shape, and elapsed time as separate evidence.
Normalize provider data at one server boundary rather than throughout the UI.

title: Recover the AtlasOps service-health dashboard

bridge.knownConcept: Redundancy, stale state, and service degradation
bridge.applicationConcept: Provider adapters, caches, revalidation, loading states, and graceful degradation
bridge.analogyLimit: Cached application data can remain intentionally usable while stale; it is not equivalent to an active redundant network path.

buildBrief: Build a typed AtlasOps dashboard showing service status, last verified time, provider source, loading, empty, error, and stale states through one adapter boundary.
incidentBrief: The upstream provider becomes unavailable while an expired cache exists. Prevent false green status, show data age, serve the safe fallback, and bound retries.

scenario.symptoms: The dashboard initially labels expired cached data as current after the provider fails.

acceptanceTests: The UI distinguishes current, stale, unavailable, empty, and loading states without relying on color
Provider-specific payloads do not reach presentation components
Retry and cache tests prove bounded behavior and visible freshness
predictionQuestions: What should the user see when stale data is safer than no data?
Where should provider-specific fields stop propagating?
defenseQuestions: Trace a refresh through route, adapter, cache, and UI.
Explain why stale must not be displayed as healthy current data.
Change the freshness threshold and update its test.
hints: Treat data value and data freshness as different fields.
Put provider translation and retry policy behind one server adapter.
Use a finite retry budget and an explicit last-verified timestamp.

title: Repair an AtlasOps row-level policy gap

bridge.applicationConcept: Relational ownership, migrations, authenticated identity, and Supabase Row Level Security
bridge.analogyLimit: RLS decisions depend on database rows, joins, identity claims, and operation type; they are not static source/destination ACL entries.

buildBrief: Model AtlasOps organizations, memberships, sites, services, maintenance windows, incidents, updates, handoffs, subscriptions, and audit events using migrations and synthetic seeds.
incidentBrief: An authenticated-select policy equivalent to unrestricted access exposes another organization’s site. Reproduce the exposure with two synthetic users, repair the policy, and add operation-specific regression tests.

scenario.symptoms: The policy simulator allows an operator in organization A to read organization B site metadata.

acceptanceTests: Migrations and seeds reproduce the documented relational model
Two-user tests fail before and pass after the organization-scoped RLS repair
Select, insert, update, and delete policy intent is documented separately
evidence: Entity diagram, migrations, and synthetic seed output
predictionQuestions: Which join proves organization membership for this row?
How could a policy pass for select but fail safely for update?
defenseQuestions: Trace authenticated identity into an RLS decision.
Explain where the ACL analogy stops being accurate.
Modify one policy test for a stakeholder role.
hints: Write the actor, action, resource, and organization before writing SQL.
Test direct data access rather than relying on a hidden page link.
Keep membership checks consistent while defining policies per operation.

title: Close an AtlasOps cross-tenant access path

bridge.applicationConcept: Authentication, organization roles, object authorization, protected routes, and signed storage access
bridge.analogyLimit: A signed-in session proves identity, not permission to every object or route in the application.

buildBrief: Add AtlasOps operator, lead, and stakeholder journeys with organization ownership, protected routes, search, filtering, and role-appropriate controls.
incidentBrief: A server route checks only that the caller is signed in before issuing access to another organization’s record. Exploit it with synthetic accounts, fix the resource boundary, and test enumeration resistance.

scenario.symptoms: An authenticated operator can request a predictable record identifier owned by a different organization.

acceptanceTests: Role journeys expose only approved actions and records
Cross-tenant direct-object requests fail at the server and database boundaries
Authorization tests cover owned, other-tenant, missing, expired, and changed-role cases
evidence: Exploit reproduction and passing regression suite
predictionQuestions: Which boundary currently proves only identity rather than ownership?
What response avoids revealing whether the other tenant’s record exists?
defenseQuestions: Trace a protected record request through route, database, and response.
Explain authentication versus authorization using the exploit.
Remove one UI control and explain why that alone is not a security fix.
hints: Test the URL or server function directly as both synthetic users.
Authorize the requested resource, action, and organization together.
Keep database policy coverage even after adding a server ownership check.

title: Contain an AtlasOps replay and prompt-injection incident

bridge.knownConcept: Authenticated control messages and replay protection
bridge.applicationConcept: Webhook signatures, idempotency, retries, structured AI output, and untrusted prompt boundaries
bridge.analogyLimit: A valid webhook signature proves origin and integrity, not that repeated business effects are safe or that payload text is trustworthy instructions.

buildBrief: Add a signed synthetic webhook, idempotent notification workflow, and bounded AI-generated shift-handoff summary with schema validation, cost limit, and deterministic fallback.
incidentBrief: A valid webhook is delivered twice while incident text contains instructions aimed at the summarizer. Prevent duplicate side effects, treat payload content as data, and fall back safely when structured output fails.

scenario.symptoms: The same signed event sends two notifications and the generated summary attempts to follow payload instructions.

acceptanceTests: Signature verification happens before processing and uses the raw synthetic body
Concurrent duplicate deliveries produce one business effect
AI output is schema-validated, budget-bounded, and replaced by a deterministic fallback on failure
predictionQuestions: Which guarantee comes from the signature and which from idempotency?
Which webhook fields must remain untrusted even when the signature is valid?
defenseQuestions: Trace a webhook from verification through one business effect.
Explain why signed content can still contain prompt injection.
Change one retry condition without allowing duplicate effects.
hints: Verify first, then atomically claim the provider event identifier.
Place payload text inside a clearly delimited data field and validate output shape.
Design the non-AI fallback before tuning the prompt.

title: Lead the AtlasOps production game day

bridge.knownConcept: Incident command, blast radius, recovery, and postmortem
bridge.applicationConcept: Application observability, environment drift, stale caches, authorization regression, rollback, and restore
bridge.analogyLimit: Application incidents include product, data, provider, and user-experience failures that infrastructure health alone may not reveal.

buildBrief: Prepare AtlasOps release checks, safe logs, health signals, backup and restore evidence, rollback instructions, ownership, privacy retention, and client handoff.
incidentBrief: A multi-fault scenario combines preview configuration drift, stale status data, a cross-tenant regression, and duplicate webhook delivery. Triage by impact, contain exposure, recover service, and write a blameless postmortem.

scenario.symptoms: Four signals appear together; one is a critical data boundary and the others affect freshness, delivery, and preview readiness.

acceptanceTests: Triage prioritizes authorization containment before lower-severity availability symptoms
Rollback and restore steps are executed against synthetic state with measured results
The postmortem separates trigger, contributing conditions, impact, detection, recovery, and prevention
evidence: Incident timeline and redacted signal captures
predictionQuestions: Which symptom creates the largest confidentiality blast radius?
Which actions contain harm before root cause is fully known?
defenseQuestions: Explain the triage order and evidence that changed it.
Distinguish rollback, restore, retry, and failover in this incident.
Identify one monitoring signal that would reduce detection time.
hints: Rank confidentiality, integrity, availability, and user impact before debugging convenience.
Contain the authorization path and preserve evidence before broad changes.
Build the timeline from observable facts and label every inference.

title: Defend the Northstar capstone launch

bridge.applicationConcept: End-to-end product defense across UI, server, database, storage, notifications, deployment, and support
bridge.analogyLimit: Passing educational security tests does not make the portal court-grade, compliance-certified, or suitable for real forensic evidence.

buildBrief: Run the Northstar preview through client, investigator, and administrator journeys; complete launch documentation, estimate, maintenance proposal, incident plan, and support handoff.
incidentBrief: The mentor game day attempts cross-client case access, expired signed-file access, unsafe audit-event mutation, provider failure, and rollback. Defend each boundary with synthetic data and evidence.
sandboxUrl: Use the Northstar Vercel preview URL recorded in the milestone PR.
fallbackUrl: Use the local Northstar project with synthetic fixtures if the preview provider is unavailable.

scenario.symptoms: Synthetic authorization, storage, audit, notification, and deployment probes exercise the complete portal.
scenario.reset: Restore the approved synthetic seed and last accepted deployment

acceptanceTests: One client cannot read another client’s cases, metadata, files, or audit events
Signed access expires and server authorization is rechecked before issuance
Launch, rollback, incident, handoff, estimate, and maintenance evidence is complete
evidence: Production and preview URLs with synthetic role matrix
predictionQuestions: Which direct-object paths could bypass the visible role dashboard?
Which evidence proves recovery without claiming legal admissibility?
defenseQuestions: Trace one case action through every trust boundary.
Explain the strongest remaining limitation to the fictional client.
Perform one controlled behavior change and repeat its security regression test.
hints: Test resources directly using two clients rather than relying on navigation visibility.
Treat storage metadata, signed URL issuance, and object access as separate controls.
Keep the educational and non-certified disclaimer visible in product and handoff material.
